# A finite grouped cap-circuit certificate

This is an exact finite geometric certificate for a strict depth failure. It
does not prove the sharp Grünbaum constant. In particular, its auxiliary
contact points are not claimed to lie in C or in S.

Assume n,d>=1. Let C be a convex body, let S=C intersect (Z^n x R^d), and
let mu be its unnormalized full mixed volume, M>0. Write
`P=pi(S)`, a nonempty finite subset of Z^n. Fix T>0 such that every point
of S has some containing closed halfspace of mu-mass strictly less than T.

Then there is the following finite certificate.

* There are s<=2^n groups, each with k_i<=d+1 nonvertical ambient caps
  `H_ij={v_ij.z+u_ij.x>=b_ij}` of mu-mass strictly less than T.
* In each group there are strictly positive multipliers lambda_ij with
  `sum_j lambda_ij=1` and `sum_j lambda_ij u_ij=0`; this is a minimal positive
  dependence, of rank k_i-1.
* Put `a_i=sum_j lambda_ij v_ij`, `h_i=sum_j lambda_ij b_ij`. Then a_i!=0.
  The inequalities `a_i.z<=h_i` jointly exclude every point of P.
* There are attained real contact points `q_i=(r_i,y_i)` such that EVERY
  selected cap inequality has nonpositive margin at q_i, and ALL inequalities
  in group i have zero margin there. Thus
  `v_ij.r_i+u_ij.y_i=b_ij`, and `a_i.r_i=h_i`.
* There are distinct integer witness points p_i in P and numbers beta_i>h_i
  such that `a_i.p_i=beta_i` and `a_j.p_i<beta_j` for j!=i. The p_i have
  pairwise distinct parity classes.

The total number of cap occurrences is at most `2^n(d+1)`. The structure is
stronger than an arbitrary cover of that size: each group has one common
attained real contact point, a minimal positive continuous-normal dependence,
and one integer witness for the expanded projected facet.

## 1. A nonempty full-dimensional auxiliary lattice-free polytope exists

Every point of the mixed lattice has depth less than T. This holds by
hypothesis on S; a lattice point outside S is outside C and can be strictly
separated from C by a zero-mass halfspace.

A containing bad cap can be chosen nonvertical with the point strictly in
its interior. First move its boundary outward a sufficiently small amount.
Continuity from above preserves the strict mass bound. The shift can be
chosen to give a boundary of mu-mass zero. A small perturbation of the normal
then makes its continuous component nonzero, preserves the interior margin,
and preserves the mass bound. For nonvertical normals, cap mass is continuous
in normal and threshold, since each within-fiber boundary hyperplane has
zero d-volume and there are only finitely many fibers.

Choose a bounded parallelepiped B containing C in its interior, whose facet
normals all have nonzero continuous components. This is possible by taking
an arbitrary basis with that property and its negatives. Its outward closed
caps have mass zero. The compact set B intersect (Z^n x R^d) is covered by
finitely many interiors of nonvertical bad caps. Intersect their complementary
closed halfspaces with B. The resulting bounded polyhedron Q_0 contains no
mixed-integer point. Every defining outward cap has mass less than T.

If Q_0 is nonempty, increasing all right-hand sides by a sufficiently small
positive amount produces a full-dimensional bounded polytope Q that remains
lattice-free. Indeed the enlarged polyhedra converge in Hausdorff distance
to Q_0: uniform boundedness follows from positive spanning of the normals,
and every convergent sequence of points satisfies the limiting inequalities.
The distance between compact Q_0 and the closed mixed lattice is positive.
Increasing thresholds only decreases cap masses.

For completeness, emptiness of Q_0 is not an unhandled case. Perturb its
normals so that every n+d of them are linearly independent, preserving their
nonverticality, positive spanning, the strict cap-mass bounds, and emptiness.
These are permitted perturbations of auxiliary inequalities, not assumptions
on C. Emptiness is stable here because
`min_w max_j(A_j.w-b_j)>0`: the maximum is coercive by positive spanning and
attains its minimum. The finite cap masses are continuous under these
perturbations.

Now increase all thresholds by a common delta until their intersection first
becomes nonempty. The critical intersection is a single point p. To see this,
its active normals have a positive dependence; otherwise a strict inward
direction would give an interior point and allow delta to decrease. A minimal
positive dependence has n+d+1 members under the imposed independence, and
those active hyperplanes determine a unique point. Moreover their positive
weighted slacks sum to zero at every feasible point, so every feasible point
lies on all of them. Hence the entire critical intersection is {p}.

Translate this critical system by an arbitrarily small vector whose integer
projection moves p off Z^n. The finite strict cap-mass margins and
nonvertical continuity preserve every bound <T. Finally increase thresholds
slightly. The resulting nonempty full-dimensional bounded Q is sufficiently
close to that translated point to avoid the mixed lattice. This proves the
claimed auxiliary-polytope existence in all cases.

## 2. Projection facets are single positive circuits

Write Q as

`Q={ (z,x): v_j.z+u_j.x<=b_j, j=1,...,N }`.

Farkas' lemma gives the exact projection description

`pi(Q)={z: sum_j lambda_j v_j.z <= sum_j lambda_j b_j
                 for all lambda>=0 with sum_j lambda_j u_j=0}`.

The cone of such multipliers is generated by its finitely many minimal
positive continuous-normal dependences. One elementary way to see this is
to intersect the cone with `sum lambda_j=1`; its vertices have precisely
minimal positive supports. Such a support has size at most d+1 and rank one
less than its size: a second independent kernel relation could perturb the
positive multiplier vector until one coordinate first vanished.

Consequently pi(Q) is defined by finitely many circuit inequalities. Since
Q is a bounded full-dimensional polytope, pi(Q) is also bounded and
full-dimensional. Each actual projection facet is therefore defined by one
of these circuit inequalities. Choose a facet description

`pi(Q)={z:a_i.z<=h_i, i=1,...,L}`,

retaining one corresponding positive circuit for each facet.

Every such facet has an attained lift q_i in Q. At that lift, the weighted
sum of the nonnegative slacks of its circuit is zero. Positivity of its
multipliers forces every constituent inequality to be active individually.
This supplies the common contact point claimed in the certificate.

## 3. A finite expansion retains at most 2^n circuits

All points p in P lie outside pi(Q). Since P is finite, choose epsilon>0
such that

`max_i(a_i.p-h_i)>epsilon` for every p in P.

Start with the expanded offsets `beta_i=h_i+epsilon`. Their polyhedron has
no point of P even on its boundary.

Increase the offsets coordinatewise, allowing the value infinity, while
requiring that the INTERIOR of the expanded polyhedron contain no point of
P. This process has a maximal endpoint using only a finite set of possible
offsets. Explicitly, if all other offsets are fixed, the largest permitted
finite value of beta_i is

`min{a_i.p : p in P, a_j.p<beta_j for every j!=i}`;

if the set is empty, remove inequality i by putting beta_i=infinity.
Each strict increase moves to one of finitely many values `a_i.p` or to
infinity. Repeating coordinate updates therefore terminates.

At termination, every retained finite facet i has a witness p_i in P with

`a_i.p_i=beta_i`, `a_j.p_i<beta_j` for all other retained j.

Different facets have different witnesses. Two witnesses cannot have the
same parity. Otherwise `(p_i+p_j)/2` is an integer point of P: it belongs
to pi(C) by convexity, hence has a nonempty C-fiber. It strictly satisfies
EVERY retained expanded inequality, contradicting interior-freeness on P.
Therefore at most 2^n facets remain.

Retain their ORIGINAL circuit inequalities `a_i.z<=h_i`. Because
`h_i<beta_i`, their joint feasible set is contained in the interior of the
expanded polyhedron. It therefore contains no point of P. The selected
circuits and their original attained contacts establish all claims above.

The expanded polyhedron is maximal for the finite relevant integer set P,
with its original facet directions. It is NOT asserted to be globally
maximal lattice-free outside pi(C). This distinction avoids an unproved
parallel-expansion or recession classification for irrational facets.

## 4. Explicit cross-circuit compatibility

The certificate contains more equations than independent group normal forms.
For all contacts q_l and all caps in group i,

`v_ij.(r_l-r_i)+u_ij.(y_l-y_i)<=0`.

After multiplying and summing, this gives

`a_i.(r_l-r_i)<=0`.

Thus each a_i supports the convex hull of ALL real contact projections at
its own r_i. These are attained common-contact inequalities, not a claim
that the contact projections are integer.

Write `delta_i=beta_i-h_i>0` and, for i!=j,
`eta_ij=beta_j-a_j.p_i>0`. The common integer term of circuit j at witness
p_i is exactly

`a_j.p_i-h_j=delta_j-eta_ij`,

while its own value is `a_i.p_i-h_i=delta_i>0`.

At any fixed integer z, the weighted sum of the defining cap margins in
group i is independent of x and equals `a_i.z-h_i`. Therefore, whenever
this quantity is positive, that group's OPEN caps cover the ENTIRE fiber
space R^d. Since every z in P violates at least one original selected
projection inequality, all selected open caps together cover S.

Each circuit admits the measure-preserving fiber shear proved in
`candidate a4ba7122ce7be4cb`, reducing its margins to a common
integer affine term plus continuous normals. Different circuits generally
require different shears; no simultaneous normalization is assumed.

## 5. What this does and does not accomplish

The plain mass consequence is only

`M <= sum_(selected cap occurrences) mu(H_ij)
    < T sum_i k_i <= T 2^n(d+1)`.

The sharper factor gamma_d does not follow from the number of groups. The
exact counterexample in `candidate a4ba7122ce7be4cb` shows that one
circuit can distribute its exclusive cap colors among distinct parity
classes and defeat a proposed gamma_d bound on that circuit's covered mass.

The real contact points q_i belong to the auxiliary Q. Their integer
coordinates r_i need not be integers, and q_i need not belong to C. They are
not candidate centers for OC. The integer witnesses p_i do have nonempty
original fibers C_(p_i), but these fibers can have zero d-volume unless a
separate positive-fiber reduction is imposed.

If the exact Tukey region D_T is nonempty, the initial finite outer
approximation can be made arbitrarily close to D_T while preserving all
strict mass bounds: cover the compact part of a fixed bounding box outside
an epsilon-neighborhood of D_T by violated bad-cap inequalities. In that
case the attained auxiliary contacts approach D_T along subsequences.
However, the corresponding normals and multipliers can have degenerate
limits, including vertical boundary-mass effects. A finite exact contact
certificate for D_T itself is NOT asserted. The counterexample in
`candidate abe945997ae088f4` shows why that additional claim
would be false in general.
